chapter: Early recordings and arrival in New York
title: Ella Fitzgerald's reaction to 'Loch Lomond' and the novelty hit
summary: Maxine says she could not be a second Ella; Ella changed her repertoire after 'Loch Lomond' and needed one hit song.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Okay, also (Inaudible) While you're playing that, we also have more recollections and comments about "Locka Loemand."

Yeah. While I was listening to the vocal, you know, I remembered when I came to New York, Ella Fitzgerald was tops, and she still is as far as I'm concerned. But I think that there was a certain similarity between my style and hers. And, of course, it's nothing to wonder about that because we're all influenced by other singers. And, of course, Ella had been a favorite of mine because even back in Pittsburgh long before I ever thought I'd be coming to New York, I used to listen to Ella's recordings. And I also listened to the broadcast from the Savoy Ballroom. And so I would think that I might've been imitating Ella up to a certain point.

However, it wouldn't done any of us any good for me to be trying to compete with Ella Fitzgerald. So I think that's one of the reasons why Claude reached out there and got "Lock Lowoud" and "Annie Laurie", to get me on another track.
If I was going to make it, I wouldn't be making it as a second Ella Fitzgerald. You know, you want to make it as one Maxine Sullivan.
But that had a curious repercussion you were just saying also.
It caused Ella to modify her repertoire.
Yeah. Ella admits that up until I did "Lock Lowoud" that she really didn't have -- I guess you would call it a gimmick -- something to identify with.
And so, after I did Lock Lowoud and it got to be such a big novelty thing, then they went out and wrote "A Tiskit A Tasket" for Ella. She admits that herself.
